questions.q: What did the famous jam study find about shoppers facing fewer varieties?
a: They were far more likely to buy when only six were shown
They spent longer deliberating over the larger display
They preferred the larger display but bought the same amount
They rated the jams as tastier when more were offered
questions.why: The overview describes Iyengar's jam study, where the smaller selection led to six times more purchases.

questions.q: According to the summary, what determines how much freedom of choice a person needs?
a: It varies by person and is strongly shaped by culture
It is highest in collectivist Eastern cultures
It stays the same for everyone once adulthood is reached
It depends mainly on income and education level
questions.why: Lesson 1 says the need for choice is highly individual, with culture named as one major factor.

questions.q: In the Space Quest study, what happened to American children who chose their own game settings?
a: They improved by 18 percent, while those denied a choice did not improve
They improved by 11 percent, less than children given the settings
They performed the same whether or not they chose
They did worse because choosing distracted them from the game
questions.why: Lesson 1 reports that the American kids gained 18 percent when they chose and not at all when they could not.

questions.q: What did the Whitehall studies suggest best explained the health gap between pay grades?
a: More freedom to structure your own work, not simply more money
Better access to private healthcare and insurance
Lower stress from having fewer responsibilities
Healthier diets and more exercise among senior staff
questions.why: Lesson 2 concludes that health was a matter of choice and control over work rather than money.

questions.q: Which parents felt best in the study about ending a terminally ill child's treatment?
a: Those who were well informed but did not have to decide themselves
Those who made the decision alone without any information
Those who were kept uninformed while the doctors stopped treatment
Those who shared the decision equally with the medical staff
questions.why: Lesson 3 says the informed group that did not choose felt best, while the uninformed and choosing groups felt equally bad.
